claims.text: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 has an FCC matrix.
The as-fabricated alloy has a uniform, fine FCC microstructure with minimal segregation.
The as-fabricated alloy has an initially intact surface oxide layer with minimal pre-existing oxidation.
Degradation in oxidizing and reducing gases is governed by element-selective oxidation at grain boundaries.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Ti preferentially oxidize at grain boundaries.
Preferential Al and Ti oxidation produces discontinuous grain-boundary oxide patches that coalesce into an oxide network.
Thermal-expansion mismatch and oxide-growth stresses associated with the grain-boundary oxide network initiate microcracks.
Microcracks generated by the oxide network propagate and can cause catastrophic failure.
Reducing conditions inhibit extensive oxide formation and therefore delay grain-boundary deterioration and overall degradation.
An inert-gas environment can be treated as a reducing condition in the proposed comparison.
Oxidizing exposure will produce more extensive grain-boundary oxidation, a thicker oxide scale, and more crack nucleation than the starting state or reducing exposure.
Oxidizing exposure will significantly reduce strength and ductility relative to the as-fabricated baseline.
Reducing exposure will substantially suppress the microstructural damage and maintain approximately baseline mechanical properties.
The proposed degradation mechanism applies at approximately 800–1000 °C during exposure times long enough for diffusion-controlled oxidation to become significant.
Lower temperatures or very short exposures may not produce degradation by the proposed grain-boundary oxidation mechanism.
The as-fabricated baseline has high mechanical performance.
